title: Costs and break-even
blurb: Fixed and variable costs, contribution margin and how many you must sell.

levels.title: Fixed and variable costs
learn: Sort a cost as fixed or variable.
Work out the unit cost and the total cost.

cards.text: Every business has costs. Some stay the same however much you sell. Some grow with every item you sell. Telling them apart is the first step to knowing whether a plan can work.
A fixed cost stays the same however many items are sold. You pay it if you sell 0 or 500. A variable cost grows with each item sold. You only pay it when you make or sell one more.
Mei sells bracelets at a weekend craft fair. The table sorts her costs. The three fixed costs add to $80.00. The variable costs are per bracelet.

The unit cost is the variable cost of one item. Mei adds beads, string and a bag: $0.90 + $0.30 + $0.20 = $1.40. The price must be higher than the unit cost, or a sale puts nothing toward the fixed costs.
Some costs hide in the wrong column. Packaging is variable: each item needs its own. A card fee charged on every sale is variable too. A banner or poster is printed once, so it is fixed.
Total cost = fixed costs + unit cost x items sold. Mei pays $80.00 even if she sells none.

questions.label: A fixed cost
questions.prompt: Which of these is a fixed cost for Mei?

terms.meaning: A cost that stays the same however many items are sold.

questions.hint: Which cost is paid once, however many bracelets she sells?

options.why: Beads are used up in every bracelet, so this cost grows with each sale.
The banner is paid once. It is the same if she sells 0 or 40 bracelets.
Each bracelet needs its own bag, so this grows with each sale.

questions.label: A variable cost
questions.prompt: Which of these is a variable cost for Mei?

terms.meaning: A cost that grows with each item sold.

questions.hint: Which cost is paid again for each bracelet?

options.why: Each bracelet uses its own string, so the cost grows with each sale.
The table is paid for once, whatever she sells.
The stand is bought once and used for every sale.
The banner is printed once, whatever she sells.

questions.label: Ravi fixed costs
questions.prompt: Ravi sells candles at a market. He has three fixed costs: the table rental, the banner and the stand. What are his fixed costs altogether?
questions.hint: Add the three amounts in the table.
questions.why: Her fixed costs are the three amounts added together.

questions.label: Candle unit cost
questions.prompt: A candle needs wax at $0.85, a wick at $0.15 and a jar at $0.60. What is the unit cost of one candle?

terms.meaning: The variable cost of one item: what it costs to make and sell one.

questions.hint: Add the three per-candle costs in the question.
questions.why: The unit cost is the variable cost of one bracelet.
questions.miss: Add only the costs paid for each candle.

questions.label: A card fee
questions.prompt: A card reader charges Mei a fee of $0.15 on every sale. Is the fee fixed or variable?

terms.meaning: A cost that grows with each item sold.

questions.hint: Does the fee happen once, or with each sale?

options.why: Size does not decide it. A cost that grows with each sale is variable.

options.text: Fixed, because the reader is bought once
options.why: The reader may be bought once, but this fee is charged again on every sale.

options.text: Variable, because it is paid on every sale
options.why: It grows with each item sold, so it is a variable cost.

questions.label: Cost of 30
questions.prompt: Mei makes and sells 30 bracelets. What is her total cost? Total cost = fixed costs + unit cost x items sold.

traps.why: That is only the variable cost. Add the fixed costs too.

questions.hint: First work out the variable cost of all 30 bracelets.
questions.why: Total cost is the fixed costs plus the variable cost of all 30.
questions.miss: Do not forget the fixed costs. Add them to the variable cost of all 30.

questions.label: Selling none
questions.prompt: Mei sells no bracelets at all. What does she still pay?

terms.meaning: A cost that stays the same however many items are sold.

questions.hint: Which costs do not depend on sales?

options.why: Fixed costs are paid whether or not anything sells.
That is one bracelet's variable cost. With no bracelets made it is not paid.
That includes variable costs for 40 bracelets, but none were made.
Fixed costs are paid even when nothing sells.

questions.label: Cost of 20
questions.prompt: Tap the bar that shows Mei's total cost for 20 bracelets.
questions.hint: Each bracelet adds the unit cost to the fixed costs.
questions.miss: Work out the total cost for 20 bracelets, then find that bar.

questions.label: A price check
questions.prompt: Tariq sells cookies for $1.20 each. Ingredients and the box cost him $1.40 a cookie. What is wrong?

terms.meaning: The variable cost of one item: what it costs to make and sell one.

questions.hint: Compare the price with the unit cost.

options.text: The price is below the unit cost, so every sale loses money
options.why: He loses $0.20 on each cookie, before any fixed costs.

options.text: The fixed costs are too high
options.why: The problem shows before fixed costs: each cookie costs more than it sells for.

options.text: Nothing, because he still has sales
options.why: Each sale brings in less than the cookie cost him to make.

options.text: The unit cost should be zero
options.why: Every cookie needs ingredients and a box, so the unit cost is not zero.

levels.title: Contribution margin and break-even
learn: Work out the contribution margin of one sale.
Find how many items cover the fixed costs.

cards.text: Jo sells iced tea at a school fair for $3.00 a cup. Each cup costs $1.10 in the cup, tea and ice. Jo's fixed costs add to $95.00.

The contribution margin is the price minus the variable cost of one item. $3.00 - $1.10 = $1.90. Each cup sold puts $1.90 toward the fixed costs. It is not profit yet. Profit starts after the fixed costs are paid.
The break-even point is the number of items a business must sell for its sales to cover all of its costs. Divide the fixed costs by the contribution margin. $95.00 / $1.90 = 50 cups.
Check it. At 50 cups Jo is even. One cup fewer and Jo is short by $1.90. One cup more and Jo makes $1.90. Break-even is the line, not a target to aim at.
A stall cannot sell part of a cup. If the answer has a decimal, round up. Say the fixed costs are $95.00 and the margin is $2.00: 47.5 so 48 cups. At 47 cups the stall is still short.
Check the margin first. If the price only equals the unit cost, the margin is $0.00. No number of sales can cover the fixed costs. If the price is lower, each sale makes the hole deeper.

questions.label: Jo's margin
questions.prompt: At the winter fair Jo sells a hot chocolate for $3.50. Each cup costs $1.30 to make. What is the contribution margin?

terms.meaning: The price minus the variable cost of one item. What each sale puts toward the fixed costs.

questions.hint: Take the variable cost away from the price.
questions.why: The margin is what each sale leaves toward the fixed costs.
questions.miss: Price minus the cost of one cup.

questions.label: Jo's fixed costs
questions.prompt: At the winter fair Jo's fixed costs are the stall fee ($55.00), the sign ($18.00) and a kettle ($12.00). What do they come to?

terms.meaning: A cost that stays the same however many items are sold.

questions.hint: Add the three fixed costs.
questions.why: The fixed costs are added together.
questions.miss: Add all three amounts. Leave out the cost of a cup.

questions.label: Break-even cups
questions.prompt: Jo's fixed costs are $95.00 and each cup leaves $1.90. How many cups must Jo sell to break even?

terms.meaning: The number of items a business must sell for its sales to cover all of its costs.

questions.hint: Divide the fixed costs by what each cup leaves.

options.why: That divides by the price of $3.00. Divide by what each cup leaves.
That divides by the cost of a cup. Divide by the margin.
That uses the dollars of fixed costs as a count of cups.

questions.label: What the margin is
questions.prompt: What is the $1.90 that each cup leaves?

terms.meaning: The price minus the variable cost of one item. What each sale puts toward the fixed costs.

questions.hint: Compare what one cup leaves with what Jo still owes in fixed costs.

options.why: Profit starts only after the fixed costs are covered.

options.text: The unit cost of a cup
options.why: The unit cost is $1.10. The margin is what is left of the price.

options.text: Money toward the fixed costs, before any profit
options.why: Each sale pays off some of the fixed costs. Profit starts after they are paid.
The fixed costs are one total. They do not grow with each cup.

questions.label: Profit at 54
questions.prompt: Jo sells 54 cups. How much profit does Jo make after paying all costs?
questions.hint: Jo is even at 50 cups. What do the cups past 50 add?
questions.why: Each cup past break-even adds the margin as profit.
questions.miss: Take the fixed costs away from the margin earned on all the cups.

questions.label: Short at 45
questions.prompt: Jo sells only 45 cups. By how much is Jo short of covering all costs?
questions.hint: Find the margin earned on 45 cups, then compare it with the fixed costs.
questions.why: Jo earns the margin on 45 cups, which is less than the fixed costs.
questions.miss: Compare the margin earned with the fixed costs, not with the sales.

questions.label: Ana's bookmarks
questions.prompt: Ana sells bookmarks for $4.00. Each costs $1.50 to make. Her fixed costs are $100.00. How many bookmarks does she need to break even?

terms.meaning: The number of items a business must sell for its sales to cover all of its costs.

questions.hint: Find her margin first. Then divide.

options.why: That divides by the price. Divide by the margin.
That divides by the unit cost. Divide by the margin.
That uses the dollars of fixed costs as a count of bookmarks.

questions.label: Rounding up
questions.prompt: A stall's fixed costs are $95.00 and its margin is $2.00. How many items must it sell to cover the fixed costs?

terms.meaning: The number of items a business must sell for its sales to cover all of its costs.

questions.hint: Divide, then think about whether part of an item can be sold.

options.why: 47 items earn $94.00, still less than $95.00.
That uses the dollars of fixed costs as a count of items.
That is the margin in dollars, not a count of items.
47.5 rounds up, because 47 items leave it short.

questions.label: Sales at break-even
questions.prompt: At break-even Ana has sold 40 bookmarks at $4.00. How much money has come in from sales?

traps.why: That is only the fixed costs. The sales also cover the cost of the bookmarks.

questions.hint: Sales are items sold times the price.
questions.why: Sales are the items sold times the price.
questions.miss: Use the price a bookmark sells for.

questions.label: No margin
questions.prompt: Noor sells pins for $2.00. Each pin costs $2.00 to make. Her fixed costs are $50.00. How many pins does she need to break even?

terms.meaning: The price minus the variable cost of one item. What each sale puts toward the fixed costs.

questions.hint: What is her margin on each pin?

options.why: That divides by the price. The margin is $0.00, not $2.00.
That uses the dollars of fixed costs as a count of pins.
The margin is $0.00, so every sale adds nothing toward the fixed costs.
With no sales she still owes the fixed costs.

levels.title: Per day, and what changes
learn: Turn break-even into a number to sell each day.
Say what a new price or cost does to it.

cards.text: Break-even in items is only half the answer. Divide it by the selling days: items ÷ days = items a day. The fair runs 5 days. Jo needs 50 cups, so 50 ÷ 5 = 10 cups a day.

Then ask if that is real. A baker's fixed costs are $360.00 and each loaf leaves $0.90, so 400 loaves. Over 10 days that is 40 a day. If about 50 people pass each day, 40 of 50 is 80%. Four in five must buy.
A lower price cuts the margin, so you need more sales. Jo drops the price by $0.50: the margin is $1.40, and $95.00 / $1.40 = 67.9, so 68 cups. Look at how fast it climbs.
Costs that go up do the same. If a cup costs $1.40 instead of $1.10, the margin is $1.60 and 59.4 rounds up to 60 cups. If the fixed costs rise to $110.00, $110.00 / $1.90 = 57.9, so 58 cups.
Test more than one result. Jo plans to sell 80 cups, so check half of that and half as much again. A plan that works only if everything goes right is a weak plan.

Items you make and do not sell are a cost you have already paid. Jo makes 80 cups and sells 60. The 20 left cost 20 x $1.10 = $22.00. Ways to cut it: a discount on the last day, or smaller batches that are made again when stock runs out.

questions.label: Cups a day
questions.prompt: Jo must sell 50 cups to break even. The fair runs 5 days. How many cups a day is that?
questions.hint: Divide the break-even cups by the number of days.

options.why: That multiplies by the days. Divide the break-even cups by them.
That subtracts the days. Divide the cups by the days.
That is the whole break-even over all days, not one day.

questions.label: Loaves a day
questions.prompt: The baker needs 400 loaves to break even over 10 selling days. How many loaves must sell each day?
questions.hint: Divide the loaves by the days.

options.why: That multiplies by the days. Divide instead.
That divides by 5 days. The stall has 10 selling days.
That is the total for all days, not one day.

questions.label: Share who buy
questions.prompt: At another stall about 50 people pass each day and the owner must sell 30 items a day, one to each buyer. What percent of the people who pass must buy?
questions.hint: Divide the sales a day by the people who pass, then write it as a percent.
questions.why: The sales a day are the share of the people passing who must buy.
questions.miss: Divide sales a day by the people who pass, then multiply by 100.

questions.label: Margin at $2.75
questions.prompt: Jo tries a price of $2.75. A cup still costs $1.10. What is the new contribution margin?

terms.meaning: The price minus the variable cost of one item. What each sale puts toward the fixed costs.

questions.hint: Price minus the cost of one cup.
questions.why: The margin falls when the price falls.
questions.miss: Use the new price, not the old one.

questions.label: Cups at $2.50
questions.prompt: At $2.50 Jo's margin is $1.40 and the fixed costs are $95.00. How many cups must Jo sell to break even?
questions.hint: Divide the fixed costs by the new margin and round up.

options.why: That is the break-even at the old price. A lower price leaves less on each cup, so more cups are needed.
That rounds down. 67 cups earn $93.80, less than $95.00.
$95.00 / $1.40 = 67.9, which rounds up to 68.
That divides by the price. Divide by the margin.

questions.label: A dearer cup
questions.prompt: Each cup now costs $1.40 and the price stays $3.00. Fixed costs are $95.00. How many cups does Jo need to break even?
questions.hint: Find the new margin first, then divide and round up.

options.why: The margin is $1.60. $95.00 / $1.60 = 59.4, rounded up.
That is the old break-even. The dearer cup lowers the margin, so more cups are needed.
That rounds down, which leaves Jo short.
That divides by the cost of a cup. Divide by the margin.

questions.label: Short at 30
questions.prompt: Jo sells only 30 cups. By how much is Jo short of covering all costs?
questions.hint: Find the margin earned on the cups sold, then compare it with the fixed costs.
questions.why: At 30 cups the margin earned is less than the fixed costs.
questions.miss: Compare the margin earned with the fixed costs.

questions.label: Profit at 90
questions.prompt: Jo sells 90 cups. How much profit does Jo make after paying all costs?
questions.hint: Margin earned on all the cups, minus the fixed costs.
questions.why: Profit is the margin earned minus the fixed costs.
questions.miss: Take the fixed costs away from the margin earned.

questions.label: Unsold cups
questions.prompt: Jo makes 90 cups and sells 65. Each cup cost $1.10 to make. What did the unsold cups cost?

terms.meaning: A cost that grows with each item sold.

questions.hint: Count the cups left over, then multiply by the cost of one.
questions.why: The unsold cups are a variable cost already paid.
questions.miss: Multiply only the cups left over by the cost of one cup.

questions.label: Money needed
questions.prompt: At which price must Jo collect the most money from sales just to break even? Each bar is the break-even cups times the price. Tap it.
questions.hint: Sales needed = cups needed x price. Compare the bars.
questions.why: At $1.50 Jo needs 238 cups, which is $357.00 in sales.
questions.miss: Compare the bars. Dropping the price raises the sales needed.
